New airports and training centres in NER 
*562. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Will the Minister of  CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Planning Commission has approved six new 
airports in the North Eastern Region including the BTAD area of Assam; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether his Ministry will contemplate policy to set up new institutes or 
training centres in some unused old airports including Rupsi of Assam on the 
lines of Pilot Training Centre, Ground Engineering Institute or Air Hostess 
Training Centre etc.; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid  on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement  
(a) and (b) The Planning Commission has approved the construction of only 
one Green-field airport in the North Eastern Region i.e. at Pekyong in Sikkim. The 
proposals for new Greenfield airports near Itanagar (Arunachal Pradesh) and at 
Cheitu (Nagaland) are under examination. 
(c) and (d) The development projects in North Eastern States are taken up at the 
request of and in consultation with North Eastern Council (NEC). There is no 
proposal from NEC for the establishment of Pilot Tr aining Institute etc. at 
Rupsi. 
The guidelines for setting up Pilot Training Instit utes and Aircraft 
Maintenance Engineering Training Institutes have already been laid down by the 
Government. 
(e) Does not arise. 
SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Sir, connectivity has been  a major 
problem in the North-Eastern region. Many times, the Civil Aviation Ministry has 
assured the people of North-East that connectivity will be improved and 
priority will be given to set up new airports. In h is reply, the hon. Minister has 
clarified that only one Green-field project has bee n approved by the Planning 
Commission in the North-Eastern region. But, in the district from which I come, 
the Bodoland Territorial District area in Assam, there is a hue and cry that a new 
airport will be set up and for that purpose, land a cquisition is also going on. 
Thousands of people are going to be evicted. There is a major problem now. We 
know that six airports have been approved by the NEC.I have come to know that the 
Planning Commission has also agreed, in principle, to set up six new airports in 
the North-Eastern region. But, I do not know the reason... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: What is your question? Please, put your question. 
SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether these six new airports are really going to be set up or not. 
And, if such proposal comes to the Ministry, what w ill be the response of the 
Ministry?

SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, hon Member ha s some 
factual data which is not in accordance with what I  have got. The Planning 
Commission has only approved one Green-field airport, and two airports —one at 
ltanagar in Arunachal Pradesh and the other at Cheitu in Nagaland — are under 
examination. The one that has been approved is a Pekyong in Sikkim. So, I do not 
know that six new airports, which he has mentioned, are at which stage. But, I 
can assure the hon. Member that as far as airports are concerned, there are 22 
operational airports already in the North-East, and  if we include Bagdogra, it 
comes to 23, and if these three airports, one-plus-two are approved, it will take 
the number to almost 26 airports. I think it is a v ast territory in terms of what 
airport you are mentioning. I do not think the Nort h-Eastern Council or the 
Planning Commission has yet given any approval for any airport, or any proposal 
for new airport is under consideration, as hon. Member has mentioned. As far as 
the Ministry is concerned, I can assure you that we are completely in agreement 
that the connectivity of the North-Eastern region s hould be maintained at the 
highest level. That is why, for all these airports,  even though there has been a 
recurring annual loss, the Airports Authority has never shied away from either 
meeting this expenditure or spending large capital expenditure for upgrading and 
developing all these airports in the North-Eastern region.

seeking bulk deposits from other banks at very high interest rates to tide over the 
liquidity problems; and 
(c) if so, the steps being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI 
PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) to (c) A statement is laid  on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement  
(a) Increased returns on competing investment products,  increase in Repo 
Rate, etc. and enhanced demand for credit, have led banks to mobilize deposits at 
higher rates of interest. 
(b) and (c) It is a normal practice for banks to borrow funds from other banks 
in the inter-bank call money market to tide over te mporary mismatches in 
their fund flows. However, to enable Public Sector Banks (PSBs) to advance 
credit to the productive sectors of the economy at reasonable rates of interest, 
the banks have been advised to increase their deposit base, with special focus on 
low-cost deposits. The performance of PSBs in this regard is also being 
monitored, on an ongoing basis, by the Government. 
SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Sir, I have seen the reply of the hon. Minister. In 
addition to that, my first supplementary is, accord ing to the press reports, the 
Government has asked the public sector banks to moderate growth of credit to 
high-risk sectors. The growth of economy continues to exert pressure on 
banks to maintain the rate of credit expansion. The  industrial sector has 
experienced a growth rate of over 8 per cent in recent months. The automobile 
industry, pharmaceuticals and the garment sector ar e enjoying robust growth. 
So, any restriction on credit expansion will result 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2007]  
into slowing down of industrial growth. Therefore, I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister whether the Government has directed the public sector banks to 
restrict credit to these sectors. 
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: Sir, there is no question of denying 
credit to any sector. The banks have only been advised to see as to which are the 
sectors and how to really modulate their credit por tfolio. The Government is 
conscious of the fact that the manufacturing sector  has played a major role in 
the growth. And, therefore, there is no denying cre dit to the manufacturing 
sector at all. 
SHRIMATI S.G INDIRA: Sir, my second supplementary is this. According to 
reports, the recovery of housing loans advanced by the public sector banks is at 99 
percent and defaulters at less than one percent. However, according to reports, the 
Government has asked the public sector banks to restrict their housing loans. It is the 
dream of an individual to have his home with the help of bank loan. Therefore, I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister whether the Government is considering to 
revise its decision on housing loans, so that the middle-class section can own house 
of its own choice. 
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: Sir, again, I would submit that there is 
no such instruction whatever that the loans to the housing sector should be 
restricted. In fact, it has been emphasised that wh ile they restructure their 
portfolios, the housing sector as such must not suffer. Rather, during the latest 
decision, the priority sector lending loan for the housing sector has been 
increased from Rs. 15,00,000 to Rs. 20,00,000.

Revealing of Participatory Notes holders names by Flls  
*564. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI † 
SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Foreign Institutional Inv estors are not bound to 
reveal the names of Participatory Notes holders whi ch goes against the well 
established concept of 'know your customers', norms practiced world over, 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Flls are not allowed  to issue PNs to Indian 
Nationals, persons of Indian origin; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(e) what steps Government have taken to ensure that terrorists operating from tax 
haven and routing their investments and wrecking ha voc on the Indian stock 
market are not allowed? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (e) A 
Statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) to (d) The Securities and Exchange Board of Ind ia (SEBI) Act, 1992 
empowers SEBI to register and regulate Foreign Inst itutional Investors 
(Flls). Under the Act, SEBI has framed the SEBI (Fl l) Regulations, 1995. 
In terms of these Regulations, an Fll may issue Par ticipatory Notes (PNs) 
with Indian instruments (equity/debt/derivative) as  the underlying securities, 
subject to the subscriber being a regulated entity.  Further downstream 
issueance of PNs, if any, can also be done to regul ated entities only. The 
Regulations also require the Flls, which issue PNs,  to file a report in a 
prescribed format at the end of each month. In this  report, amongst other 
information, the Fll has to disclose the names of a ll subscribers to the 
PNs issued by it. The reporting format also contain s an undertaking wherein 
the Fll declares that it or its associates have not  issued/subscribed/ 
purchased any PNs to/from Indian residents/NRIs/PIO s/OCBs during the 
reporting period. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of th e House by Shri Abu 
Asim Azmi. 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2007] 
(e) Adequate systems and safeguards to deal with il legal activities on the 
Indian Stock market are in place. 
The Foreign Exchange Management Act, (FEMA) 1999 has provisions to deal 
with cases of unauthorized transfer of foreign exch ange including through 
hawala.- 
The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and Rules thereunder have 
come into effect from 1st July, 2006. Under the Act and Rules, banking companies, 
financial institutions and intermediaries are oblig ed to verify the records of 
identity of clients. 
The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, as amended in September, 2004, 
has provisions to combat financing of terrorism. 
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976 (FCRA), also regulates and 
monitors receipt and use of foreign funds by the recipients. 
At the international level, India, is a member of A sia Pacific Group (APG) 
on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating of Financing of Terrorism and has 
Observer status in the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

ESOPs for employees  
*571. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT:      
SHRI RAHUL BAJAJ: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE  be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Employee Stock Option Sch emes are long-term 
benefit given to employees; 
(b) if so, how did Government initiate their coverage under Fringe Benefit Tax 
in this budget without being clear on how they would be valued and taxed; and 
(c) why they should not be more appropriately taxed in the beneficiaries hands? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) Employee 
Stock Option Schemes are undoubtedly benefits given  to employees. 
However, it is not necessary that the benefits are long-term in nature. 
(b) there is no ambiguity in the policy relating to levy of fringe benefit tax on 
Employee Stock Options Plan (ESOPs). 
(c) It is immaterial whether ESOPs are taxed in the hands of the employees 
or the employers as the applicable rate of tax would generally be same for both, 
since ESOPs are generally granted to employees in the higher tax bracket. Further 
in case ESOPs are taxed as perquisite, the employer  will be required to deduct 
TDS from the salary of the employee. On the other hand, in the case of ESOPs 
being taxed as fringe benefit, the employer has to pay the tax but it still has an 
option to recover it from the employee, without att racting any further tax 
consequences.

*572. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of PETROLE UM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received any representation from Tamil Nadu 
regarding supply of defective LPG cylinders which m ay lead to risky 
consequences; 
(b) if so, the steps taken by Government in this regard; 
(c) whether there is any mechanism to monitor the quality and standard of gas 
cylinders supplied by Indian Oil to the consumers; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI 
DEORA): (a) and (b) Government have not received an y representation from 
Tamil Nadu Government regarding supply of defective LPG cylinders by Public 
Sector Oil Marketing Companies. 
(c) to (e) At present, three Public Sector Oil Mark eting Companies 
(OMCs), namely Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOC) , Bharat Petroleum 
Corporation Limited (BPCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited 
(HPCL) are marketing LPG in the country. 
OMCs are procuring LPG cylinders from cylinder manu facturers who are 
approved by the Oil Industry Technical Committee (O ITC) and have valid 
manufacturing licences from the Bureau of Indian St andards (BIS) and the 
Chief Controller of Explosives (CCOE). Strict control is exercised by BIS over 
the manufacturing process. LPG cylinders procured by OMCs meet the required 
quality standards. 
LPG cylinders are manufactured under the close supe rvision of third party 
inspection agency, viz., BIS, which enforces strict control over the manufacturing process. 
OITC also carries out surprise audit of cylinder manufacturing units to ascertain the 
quality standards of the cylinders. Cylinders received from distributors/transporters 
at the bottling plants are mandatorily checked for quality and genuineness to avoid 
the entry of fake and outdated cylinders in circula tion. On detection, sub-
standard/spurious cylinders are confiscated and the reafter deshaped/crushed to 
prevent their re-circulation.

Amendment of income tax act  
*575. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken note of anomaly in th e matter of 
investments that qualify for reduction from income under section 80 C of the 
Income Tax Act insofar as the investments made in M utual Funds have a lock 
in period of three years whereas fixed deposits with the banks have a lock in 
period of five years; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to remove the ano maly by 
amending the Income Tax Act during the current Session; and 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2007] 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (c) 
Section 80C of the Income Tax Act provides a deduction of upto Rs. 1 lakh from 
the gross total income to an individual of HUF, which makes investments in specified 
savings instruments or makes certain specific payments. The savings instruments 
includes Equity Linked Saving Schemes (ELSS) floated by mutual funds and terms 
deposit of a scheduled bank for a period of not less than 5 years. While the lock in 
period in the case of ELSS is 3 years, it is 5 year s in the case of term deposit 
with a scheduled bank. 
Investment in ELSS is essentially an investment in equity while term deposits 
with a scheduled bank are debt instruments yielding assured returns. Therefore ELSS 
carries a significantly higher risk in comparison to a term deposit with a scheduled 
bank. In order to compensate ELSS for the higher risk, a relatively lower lock-in-
period of three years has been provided. 
In view of the above, there is no proposal to amend  Section 80C of the 
Income-tax Act.

Smuggling of antiques and statues

CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that smuggling of antiques and statues is taking place 
continuously;

foreign countries through smuggling; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that ASI is not committed  towards the 
presentation and storage of antiques of the country  and it is indifferent also 
towards the same; and

smuggling of antiques of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a) and (b) 
The availble data does not indicate continuous smuggling and illegal export of 
antiquities to foreign countries. 
(c) and (d) The Archaeological Survey of India is fully committed towards the 
conservation and safety of the antiquities at the protected monuments as well as 
the site museums. To ensure their safety, the Archa eological Survey of India 
engages security guards whose strength has been aug mented by deploying 
private security guards, State police and home guar ds personnel and also the 
CISF at selected monuments. 
Provisions exist under the antiquities and Art Trea sures Act, 1972 for 
regulation of export in antiquities and art treasur es and for prevention of their 
illicit trafficking such as registration of dealers, registration of specified categories 
of antiquities, prosecution of offenders etc. The Government is also amending the 
provisions of the Act to provide additional safety guards against illegal trafficking 
in antiquities.

2005 make it imperative on the procuring Ministries /Departments to bring 
efficiency, economy and transparency in public proc urement for fair and 
equitable treatment of suppliers and promotion of c ompetition in public

(b) whether it is a fact that rate of inflation measure s the rate of increase in 
prices and not the actual increase in prices of various items and commodities; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that wholesale price index, consumer price index, 
price index for urban non-manual employees and pric e index for agricultural 
labours do not give real picture of the situation of inflation and actual price rise; 
and 
(d) the proposed measures to know actual price rise in commodities, food 
items, vegetables and items of day to day use in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI 
PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) Sir, the average rate of growth of GDP and 
inflation (WPI based) from 1991 to 2006 is given in  the Statement (See 
below). 
(b) The rate of inflation measures the rate of increase  in prices and is 
calculated on the basis of an index consisting of various commodities and having 
a weight assigned to each commodity. Based on the r ate of increase in price 
of each commodity and the weight assigned to that c ommodity in the basket, a 
composite rate of inflation is calculated. There ar e, at present, five such 
composite rates of inflation, viz. (i) Wholesale Pr ice Index (WPI), (ii) 
Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW ), (iii) Consumer Price 
Index for Urban Non-Manual Employees (CPI-UNME), (i v) Consumer Price 
Index for Agricultural Labour (CPI-AL) and (v) Consumer Price Index for Rural 
Labour (CPI-RL). 
(c) In case of WPI, the basket is only of selected commodities and the weight 
assigned to each commodity is on the basis of the value of traded amount of that 
commodity. The other indices, which are all variant s of the Consumer Price 
Index, are based on the consumption pattern of the different groups, thereby 
implying different weights assigned to a particular commodity or services in the 
respective baskets. 
(d) In view of the divergent factors affecting the dema nd and supply of a 
particular commodity in different regions of the co untry, it is not possible to 
have a unique measure of the rise in price of a particular commodity for the entire 
country.

Statement  
Details Of New Initiaves Taken To Check Adulteration Of Petrol/ Diesel 
And Streamlining Pds Kerosene Distribution  
Checking adulteration is a continuous process and t he Ministry of 
Petroleum & Natural Gas has been reviewing steps ta ken to curb adulteration 
from time to time. In the process, several technolo gical and institutional 
measures have been taken to contain adulteration. T he recent steps taken by 
the Ministry are summerized below. 
1. Automation of Retail Outlets: In order to monitor t he activities at retail 
outlets by adopting the latest technological improvements, automation of retail 
outlets is being implemented. MOP&NG has directed t he oil marketing 
companies to complete automation of retail outlets selling more than 200 KL per 
month. 
2. Third Party Certification of Retail Outlets: OMCs h ave been directed to 
complete third party certification of all the retail outlets selling more than 100 
KL per month. 
3. Monitoring of movement of Tank Trucks through Globa l Positioning 
System (GPS): In order to prevent adulteration duri ng transportation, OMCs 
have been directed to install GPS for complete moni toring of the movement 
of all the company owned/dealer owned/ contractor owned tank trucks. 
4. Marker System in Kerosene: To check adulteration in  auto fuels, 
Government has asked public sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) to take 
various steps, including introduction of marker in adulterants. OMCs have 
commenced introduction of marker in kerosene on all  India basis with effect 
from 1.10.2006. Under the new system, Market is being put in kerosene in all 
depots. This system heralds the introduction of wor ld class technology to curb 
and eventually eliminate the menance of adulteratio n of transportation fuels 
along the supply chain. With the marker's presence, aduteration even with very 
low levels of kerosene can be detected. MS/HSD Cont rol Order, 2005 SKO 
Control Order, 1993 and MDG 2005 have been amended for making provision 
regarding introduction of marker system in Kerosene to check adulteration. A 
committee has been set up in the Ministry to monitor the progress of the marker 
system. Oil Marketing Companies in the Private Sector have also been 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2007] 
simultaneously asked to introduce marker in Kerosene as is being done by 
Public Sector OMCs. 
5. Revising the Marketing Discipline Guidelines: The M arketing 
Discipline Guidelines (MDG) under which the oil mar keting companies take 
penal actions against the erring dealers have been revised during August 2005 
making the penal actions more stringent. As per MDG, 2005, a dealership would be 
terminated in the first instance of adulteration itself. 
6. Jan Kerosene Pariyojna: To streamline the PDS Kerosene distribution system 
and contain diversion of kerosene for adulteration and other unauthorized 
usages, Jan Kerosene Pariyojna (JKP) had been launched initially for a period of 
6 months on a pilot basis in 414 blocks with effect  from 2.10.2005. The Pilot 
scheme has been further extended upto 30.6.2007. 
7. Smart Card Scheme: With the objective of ensuring that the benefit of the 
subsidy reaches the targeted consumers in an efficient and cost-effective manner 
and to prevent any leakages, this Ministry has prop osed introduction of Smart 
Card System for distribution of PDS kerosene. The s cheme is proposed to be 
introduced initially on an experimental basis. In t he Pilot project, subsidized 
kerosene through Smart Card is proposed to be evailable to BPL families while all 
other ration card holders would be given non-subsidized kerosene. Oil Marketing 
Companies (OMCs) would ensure adequate availability of PDS as well as non-
subsidized kerosene during the entire period of implementation of the Pilot.

Constitution of Heritage Sites Commission  
4409.    SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA:                                      
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR:  
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government proposes to constitute a Heritage Sites Commission 
as the present legal and institutional framework is  inadequate to address the 
conservation of built heritage in its broadest outline; 
(b) whether the function of the proposed Heritage Sites Commission would 
include advising Government on heritage matters and  framing guidelines for 
conservation of heritage monuments and sites; and 
(c) if so, by when Government is likely to announce its formation? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. As the present legal and institutional fr amework is not adequate to 
address the documentation, inventorisation and conservation of built heritage in 
its broadest outline, government has proposed to co nstitute a Heritage Sites 
Commission. The Commission would lay down broad policy guidelines and take 
steps to ensure that such guidelines are observed. 
The functions of the proposed Heritage Sites Commission would include: 
— tender advice to Government on heritage matters. 
— frame guidelines in the matter of conservation of heritage 
monuments and sites. 
— study or cause to study important matters regarding conservation of 
heritage and submit reports to the Government. 
— suggest appropriate amendments to the existing heritage 
legislations. 
(c) No time frame can be indicated at this stage.

[15 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Water crisis  
†4421. SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: Will the Minister fo r WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are formulating any plan to solv e the problem of 
water crisis; and 
(b) if so, the details thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) The 
average annual water availability in the country is assessed a 1869 billion cubic 
metre (BCM). Based on the population of 1027 millio n as per the 2001 
census, the per capita available works out to be 18 20 cubic metre per year. 
However, there is considerable temporal and spatial  variations in the water 
availability in the country and due to population g rowth, the per capita water 
availability is also declining year after year. The re are also instances of over-
exploitation of ground water leading to lowering of water table in certain areas. 
Water being a state subject, several measures for d evelopment and 
management of water resources are undertaken by the  respective State 
Governments which include creation of storages, res toration of water bodies, 
rain water harvesting, artificial recharge to ground water and adoption of better 
management practices etc. Government of India provi des assistance to the 
State Governments for completion of on-going irriga tion projects under the 
Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP). Further, a pilot scheme titled 
"National Project for Repair, Renovation and Restor ation of Water Bodies 
directly linked to Agriculture" has been approved b y Government of India in 
January 2005. Government of India also provides sup port under centrally 
sponsored scheme for Command Area Development and W ater Management 
(CAD&WM) with a view to bridging the gap between ir rigation potential 
created and potential utilized. Government has also constituted an Advisory Council 
on Artificial Recharge to Ground Water under the Ch airmanship of Union 
Minister of Water Resources with the main objective to popularize the concept 
of artificial recharge to ground water among all stakeholders.

RAJYA SABHA [15 May, 2007] 
Cost of delay in irrigation projects  
4422. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Centre and the States are losing over a lakh crore rupees 
due to cost over-runs in delayed irrigation projects; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that about 205 major and minor irrigation projects which 
originally would have cost Rs. 1,10,242 crore due to delays ranging from one to six 
years; and 
(c) if so, whether Government have made any investigations to find the cause for delay 
and the action proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) Delay in 
completion of projects results in cost over-run. The other reasons for cost over run are 
inadequate provision in the original estimates, change in the scope of the project mostly 
extension of command area, geological surprises, unexpected increase in the cost of land 
acquisition, Resettlement and Rehabilitation, forest land acquisition,cost escalation of 
construction material, labour etc. In view of normal gestation period of major projects as 10 
to 15 years and that of medium projects as 5 to 8 years, the major projects started during 
or before 1992 and medium projects started during or before Eighth plan which will be 
continuing as ongoing in Eleventh plan may be" considered as delayed projects. As per the 
Working Group Report for Eleventh Plan, Plan-wise break-up of such ongoing projects 
likely to spill over into Eleventh Plan are given as under:.

Statement  
Recommendations made by the sub-committee headed by 
Dr. M.S. Swaminathan 'more crop and  
income per drop of water'  
The report of the Sub-committee on 'more crop and income per drop of water' 
highlights that the irrigation water security is vital both for livelihood and food 
security. The report draws attention to the scope a vailable for improving the 
efficiency of use of irrigation water in a manner that both the productivity and 
profitability of farming are enhanced which is the pathway to an ever-green 
revolution all over the country, without associated ecological harm. Important 
recommendations of the Sub-Committee are as follows:— 
* The Sub-Committee recommended observation of Year 2007-08 as the 
'Year of More Crop and Income per Drop of Water to give the strategies 
and their importance in improving the productivity and income per 
unit of water. 
* Adequate provisions in XI Plan for inclusion of the  measures for 
augmentation of water supply should be made. The investment from 
Government as well as from lending Agencies such as World Bank should 
give priority for modernization of the tertiary can als with control 
structures.

* Micro Irrigation technology e.g. drip and sprinkler  irrigation 
including drip fertigation to increase productivity of crops with less 
water should also be popularized. System of Rice In tensification 
technology (SRI) which requires less quantity of se eds, less nursery 
area, saves water and labour and enhance yield is also required to be 
popularized. 
* Introduction of weather based crop insurance for minimizing the losses 
to farmers for safeguarding farmers during weather uncertainties. 
* Implementation of Farmer Participatory Action Resea rch 
Programmes with the help of Agricultural Universiti es, Research 
Institutes, ICRISAT, WALMIs, etc. for triggering a mass 
movement. This Programme can cover 5000 villages in different agro-
climatic regions during 2007-08. The Gram Sabhas in the villages will 
serve as Pani-panchayats and will provide overall g uidance and 
support to this programme. In addition, launching o f water literacy 
movement' and imparting training to one woman and man from every 
panchayat as Water Masters is also suggested. 
* The Water User Agencies (WUAs) should be involved i n the 
decision making so that the maintenance of the stru ctures will be 
made easy. 
* In order to implement successfully the above recommendations, a 3-tier 
setup at Village, State and National level has been  suggested. At 
National level, a Pan Government of India Steering Committee 
consisting of representatives of various Departments which will report 
to-Agricultural Cordination Committee, chaired by t he Prime 
Minister.

4426. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Central Ground Water Auth ority (CGWA) have 
been constituted to regulate and control ground wat er management and 
development; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) how far Central Ground Water Authority has achieved  the target to 
regulate and control ground water; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) what concrete steps Government propose to take to solve the shortage of 
ground water and river in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and(b) Yes 
Sir. Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has been constituted under sub-
section 3 of Section 3 of the Environment (Protecti on)Act,1986 vide & 
notification dated 14.01.1997 and subsequent amendments for the purpose of 
regulation and control of ground water development and management in the 
country. 
(c) The Central Ground Water Authority has undertak en the following 
regulatory measures to control the development of ground water. 
(i) Central Ground Water Authority is regulating withdrawal of ground . 
water by industries/projects in 1065 over-exploited , critical and semi-
critical areas. List of these areas has been circul ated to the State 
Pollution Control Boards and Ministry of Environment & Forests which 
refer the new industries/projects falling in these areas to CGWA for 
obtaining permission. Pre-conditions in case of permissions are mandatory 
adoption of rain water harvesting system, monitoring of ground water 
abstraction as well as monitoring of ground water l evel and quality etc. 
by the industry. 
(ii) CGWA has notified 43 Over-exploited areas in t he country for 
regulation of ground water development and manageme nt. For 
enforcement of the regulatory directions Issued under Section 5 
220 

[15 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
of EPA. 1986, concerned Deputy Commissioners/ Distr ict 
Magistrates have been authorized to take necessary action in case of 
violation of directives of CGWA in the notified areas. In these notified 
areas, installation of new ground water abstraction structures is not 
permitted without prior specific approval of the Authority. For more 
effective regulation of ground water development and management, 
Advisory Committee under the Chairmanship of Distri ct 
Collector/Deputy Commissioners have been constituted. 
(iii) Directions have been issued Group Housing Societies, Institutes, Hotels, 
Industries, Farm Houses, etc. in the notified areas  of Delhi, 
Faridabad, Gurgaon and Gaziabad and other areas of NCT Delhi where 
ground water table is below 8 metres from ground su rface to adopt 
roof top rain water harvesting system. The last date for adoption of 
rain water harvesting has been extended upto 30.06.2007. 
(iv) CGWA have also notified 65 over-exploited areas in various States for 
registration of ground water abstraction structures , which showed a 
very steep decline in ground water levels and requi red action for 
regulation. 
(d)Does not arise. 
(e) Several measures for development and management  of irrigation are 
undertaken by the respective State Governments whic h include creation of 
storages, restoration of water bodies, rain water h arvesting, artificial recharge 
to ground water and adoption of better management p ractices etc. 
However,Government of India is providing Central As sistance to the State 
Governments through various schemes/programmes, suc h as Accelerated 
Irrigation Benefits Programmes (AIBP); Command Area  Development and 
Water Management (CADWM) Programme; National Projec t for Repair, 
Renovation and Restoration of Water Bodies directly linked to Agriculture etc. 
The Government of India also encourages rain water harvesting and recharge to 
ground water for conservation of water. The Central  Ground Water Board 
(CGWB), under the Ministry of Water Resources, has also circulated 
Manual/Guide on Artificial Recharge to Ground Water  to the States/Union 
Territories to enable them to formulate area specific artificial recharge schemes 
to check the declining trend of

Interlinking of rivers 
4430. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of WA TER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the world experts have pointed that water flow on glacier-fed rivers will 
decrease substantially in the coming decades due to the effect of global warming; 
(b) whether India propose to have any contingency plan in place by inter-linking 
of its rivers; and 
(c) what follow-up action has been taken on our river inter-linking policy and now many 
agreements have been signed for such projects so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) A number of reports 
about the effect of climate change and global warming on water flow have been published 
from time to time. Some of these reports indicate reduction of flows in glacier-fed rivers. 
The report titled "India's Water Economy bracing for a turbulent future" by World Bank 
states that "Climate change is likely to substantially increase overall monsoonal rainfall in India, 
but this is liekly to be poorly distributed in the sense that much of the additional rainfall 
will probably be in high-intensity storm events". 
(b) and (c) The Government of India have formulated a National Perspective Plan 
for Water Resources Development (NPP) in August 1980. The NPP comprises of two 
components viz. (i) Peninsular Rivers Development and (ii) Himalayan Rivers 
Development and envisages construction of storages on various river system along with 
interlinking canal systems to transfer water from water surplus area to water deficit 
regions. National Water Development Agency (NWDA) under Ministry of Water 
Resoruces has been set up in 1982 to study the feasiblity of inter basin water transfer 
proposals and give a concrete shape to NPP. NWDA after various studies identified 30 links 
under NPP (16 Peninsular and 14 Himalayan) for preparation of feasiblity reports. So 
far, NWDA has completed the feasibilities reports for 14 links under Peninsular Component-
and 2 links under Himalayan Component. A tripartite agreement (MoU) between the 
Government of India and concerned States of Madhya Pradesh & Uttar Pradesh was signed on 
25.03.2005 for preparation of Detailed Project Report (DPR) for the Ken-Betwa link under 
Peninsular Component.

Incidence of cross-border Intrusion  
†*581 . DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether incidence of cross-border intrusions by  foreign intruders in 
various States of the country is on the decline; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [16 May, 2007] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the borders of the country which are highly vulnerable to intrusions and 
the reasons therefor, and 
(d) the details of measures taken by Government to check intrusions? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): (a) to 
(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) Available information about apprehension of for eign intruders etc. 
indicates a decline in cross-border infiltration on  the Indo-Pakistan and Indo-
Bangladesh borders. There is no significant incidence of cross-border intrusion of 
foreigners on the indo-Bhutan, Indo-Nepal, Indo-Mya nmarand India-China 
borders. 
(b) The details of apprehension of foreign intruder s on Indo-Pakistan and 
Indo-Bangladesh International Borders during the last three years are as under:

(c) Indo-Bangladesh border is vulnerable to infiltr ation on account of poor 
economic conditions on Bangladesh side; porous and riverine border; high density 
of population in Bangladesh; and cultural, religiou s, linguistic and ethmic 
similarities among the people living on either side of the border. Indo-Pakistan 
border is also vulnerable to terrorist infiltration. 
(d) The Government have adopted a multi-pronged approach to contain cross-
border intrusions by foreign nationals which includ es, inter alia, round the 
clock surveillance of the border by patrolling and by establishing observation 
posts; construction of border fencing and flood lig hting; introduction of 
modern and hi-tech surveillance equipment; upgradation of intelligence set up 
and coordination with the State Governments and con cerned intelligence 
agencies.

for the farming activities in that particular area reqularly, as a result of which 
the farmers are facing problems everyday. Many times, Sir, the BSF people are 
also firing on our own citizens. Therefore, through  you, sir, I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister as to what action has b een taken to make the 
system easy, so that our farmers are able to go to that particular area and do the 
farming activities.

RAJYA SABHA [16 May, 2007] 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, this is the real problem which is faced 
by the farmers in that area because the land which belongs to them is on the other 
side of the fence and on this side of the international border. In fact, we have given 
them the outlets and they can go through the doors and the passages into the land; 
they can cultivate the land and they can come back.  As far as my information 
goes, there have been some incidents where this thing might have happened and 
has happened also. But, by the large, they are satisfied and our people are helping 
them to go there and come back. In fact, they are w anting more doors to be 
opened. They are asking the doors to be kept opened throughout the day and the 
night and things like that. We will definitely take  steps to see that they are 
facilitated in doing that. They are really facing the difficulties because the inlets, 
the doors, the passages which can take the farmers from this side into their land 
are also limited. We would like to have more such passages provided to them, and 
if there is anything else which has to be done, we would be only happy to 
consider it for a favourable action.

DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, what t he hon. 
Minister has mentioned is the tip of the iceberg. He has mentioned numbers of only 
those who have been arrested, but not those Banglad eshis who have intruded 
and escaped arrest. According to general perception , there are two crore of 
Bangladeshi intruders in the country which is the m ost potent threat to the 
sovereignty, integrity and secularity of this country. The demographic pattern 
in all the seven Eastern States is changing because  of this. When General 
Sinha was the Governor of Assam, he had made a very  specific report on this 
account. The Intelligence Agencies have also made a report. I have got a report 
with me, Sir. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Don't quote the report. 
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: But in that it is written , "Bangladeshi 
border, which is 4,039 kilometres, being porous, is  one of the most 
threatening borders from where they are coming." I would like to know 
specifically how alarming is the situation. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: What is your question? 
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Sir, my question is, how alarming is the 
situation of Bangladeshi intruders? What is their real number? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, let us not make this si tuation appear to be 
alarming ...(Interruptions)... The situation is controllable, and we are quite 
confident to control it. But if we take a stand which is not in tune with the reality 
as such, but it is a political stand, then it appea rs to be or if is made to appear 
alarming; we should not do that. Problem is there. We are in a position to solve it, 
and we are trying to solve it under the Foreigners Act and the other Acts with the 
help of accords with the State Governments also. As far as stopping the infiltration 
is concerned, it is the responsibility of the Union Government. I have already said 
in reply to the first question. But, as far as detecting and then taking the cases 
to the courts is concerned, it has to be done. May I explain to you that if you 
detect the

and we are trying to solve this human problem ...(Interruptions)...  
SHRIMATIBRINDA KARAT: The hon. Member wants to know whether the 
figure is two crores. He has mentioned the figure. 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATH: I do not think that number is  correct. The 
number should not be quoted unnecessarily, to make the issue alarming

[16 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Uniform criteria for DTH companies and pay channels 
*582. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that according to TRAI regulat ions for CAS, each 
consumer must pay a maximum of Rs. 5 for every pay channel, while there is 
no such stipulation for DTH, as the regulator belie ves competition provides 
sufficient price control; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government are taking any action to provide level playing field 
and enforce uniform criteria for the DTH companies to offer channels as per the 
choice of viewers; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND THE MINISTER 
OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has informed that in large 
parts of the country, the incumbent cable TV services are not required by regulatory 
mandate to provide their services through an addressable system. CAS has been 
mandated for cable TV services in notified areas which is a very limited part of 
the country. Throughout the non-CAS areas, the incu mbent cable television 
operators, who enjoy the dominance in the market, a re not required by any 
regulatory mandate to introduce an addressable system. Therefore, regulation of 
pricing for DTH services is likely to be interpreted to mean that the new entrant 
DTH operators are asymmetrically regulated against the incumbent mode of 
delivery, which has dominant market share. 
(c) and (d) The cable TV network services which have dominant market share 
are not required by any regulatory mandate to intro duce addressable systems. 
Therefore, Government do not think it fit to regula te pricing for DTH services 
which have inbuilt addressable system. However, TRAI is free to intervene at any 
point of time against any retail or wholesale tariff of DTH operators in any part of 
country if such tariff packages are found to be not  consumer friendly or not 
transparent in the offer.

Safeguarding the Interests of Indian farmers in ASEAN  
*587. DR. ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Association of South East Asian Nations  (ASEAN) had 
attended to the sensitivities of India during the n egotiations held during 
January, 2007 in Philippines, for the proposed Free Trade Agreement (FTA); 
(b) if so. whether India's objective of forging a consensus with the ASEAN 
on the contentious issues of the negative list of items that we did not want to be 
considered, was adequately achieved; and 
(c) whether the interests of Indian farmers and section s of the deomestic 
industry have been safeguarded? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir . ASEAN 
Economic Ministers (AEM)-lndia Consultations Meeting was held at Cebu, 
Philippines on January 11, 2007, during which both ASEAN and India agreed 
to maintain a Negative List to cover their respective sensitivities. It was further 
agreed that the Negative List by India and each ASE AN Member country 
would be subject to a maximum number of 490 tariff lines and an import value 
cap of 5%. Even though ASEAN were initially disincl ined to accept India's 
proposed for a Negative List, India was able to persuade ASEAN to provide for 
mutally agreed sensitivities through a Negative List. 
(c) India's proposed Negative List adequately safeg uards the interests of 
farmers and sensitive sectors of the domestic indus try. The Negative List 
consists of items mostly of Agricultural products, Textiles, Chemicals and Petro-
chemicals, Automobiles etc. The negative list has b een made in consultation 
with various Ministries and other stakeholders.

Rehabilitation measures for child labour  
*594.SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARATAIMUR: 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what effective and comprehensive measures have been  adopted by 
Government after ban on child labour came into forc e, to ensure that the 
rescued children are properly looked after and give n vocational or any other 
training so that they become self-sufficient in course of time; 
(b) what long-term plans for proper enforcement and rehabilitation have been 
drawn by Government, in consultation with State Governments and NGOs, etc. 
in this regard; and 
(c) what has been, the financial implications towards t his rehabilitation 
programme during the three months it has been in existence? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE (INDEPENDENT CHARGE) OF THE 
MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR 
FERNANDES): (a) Under the Child Labour (Prohibition  & Regulation) Act, 
1986, employment of children is prohibited in hazar dous Occupations and 
Processes. At present, there are 15 such occupation s and 57 processes 
prohibited under the Act. These include two occupat ions i.e. employment of 
children as domestic workers or servants and employment of children in dhabas 
(road-side eateries), restaurants, hotels, motels, tea-shops, resorts, spas or 
other recreational centers which have been added re cently in the list of 
occupations w.e.f. 10.10.06. For the rehabilitation of children withdr awn 
from work, the Government is implementing the Natio nal Child Labour 
Project (NCLP) Scheme in 250 districts of 20 States of the country. Under the 
scheme, children withdrawn from work are put into the special schools where 
they are provided with education, nutrition, stipend, health care etc Vocational 
Training is also 
41 

.     RAJYA SABHA [16 May, 2007] 
one of the very important component under the schem e. These children are 
provided with skills which are necessary for them t o earn better livelihood 
later in their lives. 
(b) and (c) As the State Governments are the approp riate Government for 
implementation of the Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986, in their 
respective areas, they have been advised to take all appropriate measures for the 
effective implementation of the recent ban. In this  connection, the then Union 
Labour Minister had taken up with all the Chief Ministers for creating awareness 
generation and effective enforcement of the ban. Government of India also held 
consultations with the State Governments, NGOs, and  other stake holders at 
Zonal level conferences held all over the country d uring the months of 
September and October, 2006. During these Zonal Con ferences at Bangalore 
(Southern Zone), Guwahati (North East Zone), Ranchi  (Eastern Zone), 
Amritsar^Northern Zone) and Goa (Western Zone), the  State Governments 
discussed their action plans for effecting the ban and for the rehabilitation of these 
children. NGOs and other members of the civil society were also requested during 
the consultations for their suggestions as also to supplement the efforts of the 
Government in creating awareness generation, and pr oviding rehabilitation in 
terms of food, clothing and shelter. The effectiven ss of measures adopted by 
States was reviewed in January, 2007. Government has also formed a Core Group 
for convergence of Ministry of Labour and Employmen t with various other 
Ministries viz., Ministry of Women and Child Development, Human Reso urce 
Development, Rural Development, Urban Housing and Poverty Alleviation and 
Social Justice and Empowerment for the rehabilitation of child labour and their 
families under the welfare schemes of these ministries also. Under the Scheme of 
National Child Labour Projects (NCLP) Rs. 108 crores were spent for the rehabilitation 
of child labour during the last financial year.

Achievement of WTO objectives at Doha  
†4457. SHRI MAHENDRA SAHNI: Will the Minister of CO MMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have achieved the prime objectives of the draft Doha 
agreement of World Trade Organisation of August, 2004; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that many differences bet ween the Ministry of 
Agriculture and Ministry of Commerce have arisen about the number of products 
to be kept in the category of special products, for  providing protection to agro 
products against import on cheaper rates under the Agreement on Agriculture 
of World Trade Organisation; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof, alongwith the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) The negotiating mandate 
agreed by consensus of all WTO Members, including India, is contained in the 
Doha Ministerial Declaration of 14 November 2001, a s elaborated and 
complemented by the General Council Decision of 1 A ugust 2004 (the 
"Framework") and the Hong Kong Ministerial Declaration of 18 December 2005. 
In the elements and principles agreed thus far India has been able to secure 
recognition that agriculture is of critical importance to the economic development 
of developing country Members and that they must be able to pursue agricultural 
policies that are supportive of their development g oals, poverty reduction 
strategies, food security and livelihood concerns. Accordingly, some elements of 
special and differential treatment for developing c ountries have already been 
agreed, including the right to self-designate an ap propriate number of Special 
Products (SPs) for more flexible treatment, and a Special Safeguard Mechanism 
(SSM) which would be designed to address surges in imports and international 
price declines. In domestic support, it has been agreed that developing countries 
like India will be exempted from any reduction in t he trade-distorting domestic 
support provided to its farmers. It has also been agreed that developing countries 
like India could continue to provide marketing and transport subsidies on 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
71 

RAJYA SABHA [16 May, 2007] 
exports for a further period of five years beyond the elimination of all forms of 
export subsidies by WTO Members. 
The Framework reaffirms the importance of special a nd differential 
treatment in non-agricultural market access (NAMA) and these negotiations will aim 
at reduction or as appropriate elimination of tariffs including tariff peaks, high 
tariff peaks and tariff escalations in particular i n products of export interest to 
developing countries, as well as non-tariff barrier s. The bound tariff reduction 
commitments of developing countries will be based on the principle of 'less than 
full reciprocity' as compared to those of the developed countries. Flexibilities to 
address the senstivities of developing countries will be developed further in the 
negotiations. 
(c) and (d) The agricultural products to be self-de signated as Special 
Products by developing countries, including India, would be based upon the 
negotiated outcome of the Doha Work Programme, whic h will establish the 
modalities including indicators to guide the self-d esignation of an appropriate 
number of tariff lines as Special Products based on the criteria of food security, 
livelihood security and rural development. The question of differences between 
the Department of Agriculture and Cooperation and t he Department of 
Commerce, therefore, does notarise.

OFFICE MEMORANDUM  
Subject: North East Industrial and Investment Promotion Policy  
(NEIIPP), 2007  
The Government has approved a package of fiscal inc entives and other 
concessions for the North East Region namely the 'N orth East Industrial and 
Investment Promotion Policy (NEIIPP), 2007, effective from 1.4.2007, which, 
inter-alia, envisages the following: 
(i) Coverage: 
The North East Industrial Policy (NEIP), 1997 annou nced on 24.12.1997 
covered the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, 
89 

RAJYA SABHA [16 May, 2007] 
Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. Under NEIIPP, 2007, Sikkim will also be 
included. Consequently, the 'New Industrial Policy and other concessions for the 
State of Sikkim' announced vide O.M. No. 14(2)/2002-SPS dated 23.12.2002 
and the Schemes thereunder i.e. Central Capital Investment Subsidy Scheme, 
2002, Central Interest Subsidy Scheme, 2002 and Central Comprehensive Insurance 
Scheme, 2002, notified vide Notification No. F. No. 14(2)/2002-SPS dated the 
24.12.2002 will be discontinued from 1.4.2007. 
(ii) Duration:  
All new units as well as existing units which go in  for substantial 
expansion, unless otherwise specified and which com mence commercial 
production within the 10 year period from the date of notification of NEIIPP, 2007 
will be eligible for incentives for a period of ten  years from the date of 
commencement of commercial production. 
(iii) Neutrality of location:  
Incentives will be available to all industrial units, new as well as existing units 
on their substantial expansion, located anywhere in the North Eastern Region. 
Consequently, the distinction between 'thrust' and 'non-thrust' industries made 
in NEIP, 1997 will be discontinued from 1.4.2007. 
(iv) Substantial expansion:  
Incentives on substantial expansion will be given t o units effecting 'an 
increase by not less than 25% in the value of fixed  capital investment in plant 
and machinery for the purpose of expansion of capac ity/modernization and 
diversification', as against an increase by 33 1/4% which was prescribed in NEIP, 
1997. 
(v) Excise Duty exemption:  
100% Excise Duty exemption will be continued, on finished products made 
in the North Eastern Region, as was available under NEIP, 1997. However, in 
cases, where the CENVAT paid on the raw materials and intermediate products 
going into the production of finished products (other than the products which are 
otherwise exempt or subject to nil rate of duty) is  higher than the excise duties 
payable on the finished products, ways and means to  refund such overflow of 
CENVAT credit will be separately notified by the Ministry of Finance. 
90 

[16 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(vi) Income Tax exemption:  
100% Income Tax exemption will continue under NEIIP P, 2007 as was 
available under NEIP, 1997. 
(vii) Capital Investment Subsidy:  
Capital Investment Subsidy will be enhanced from 15% of the investment in 
plant and machinery to 30% and the limit for automatic approval of subsidy at 
this rate will be Rs. 1.5 crores per unit, as against Rs.30 lakhs as was available 
under NEIP, 1997. Such subsidy will be applicable t o units in the private 
sector, joint sector, cooperative sector as well as  the units set up by the State 
Governments of the North Eastern Region. For grant of Capital Investment 
Subsidy higher than Rs. 1.5 crore but upto a maximum of Rs.30 crores, there will 
be an Empowered Committee Chaired by Secretary, Dep artment of Industrial 
Policy & Promotion with Secretaries of Department of Development of North 
Eastern Region (DONER), Expenditure, Representative  of Planning 
Commission and Secretary of the concerned Ministries of the Government of India 
dealing with the subject matter of that industry as  its members as also the 
concerned Chief Secretary/Secretary (Industry) of the North Eastern State where the 
claiming unit is to be located. 
Proposals which are eligible for a subsidy higher than Rs. 30 crores, will be 
placed by Department of Industrial Policy and Promo tion before the Union 
Cabinet for its consideration and approval. 
(viii) Interest Subsidy:  
Interest Subsidy will be made available @ 3% on working capital loan under 
NEIIPP, 2007 as was available under NEIP, 1997. 
(ix) Comprehensive Insurance  
New industrial units as well as the existing units on their substantial 
expansion will be eligible for reimbursement of 100% insurance premium. 
(x) Negative List:  
The following industries will not be eligible for b enefits under NEIIP, 
2007:- 
(i) All goods falling under Chapter 24 of the First  Schedule to the 
Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 (5 of 1986) which p ertains to 
tobacco and manufactured tobacco substitutes. 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [16 May, 2007] 
(ii) Pan Masala as covered under Chapter 21 of the First Schedule to the 
Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 (5 of 1986) 
(iii) Plastic carry bags of less than 20 microns as specified by Ministry of 
Environment and Forests Notification No, SO. 705(E)  dated 
02.09.1999 and S.O. 698(E) dated 17.6.2003. 
(iv) Goods falling under Chapter 27 of the First Schedule to the Central Excise 
tariff Act, 1985 (5 of 1986) produced by petroleum oil or gas 
refineries. 
(xi) Incentives for Service/other Sector Industries 
• Incentives under NEIIR 2007 will be applicable to the following service sector 
activities/industries:— 
I. Service Sector: 
(i) Hotels (not below Two Star category), adventure  and leisure sports 
including ropeways; 
(ii) Medical and health services in the nature of n ursing homes with a 
minimum capacity of 25 beds and old-age homes, 
(iii) Vocational training institutes, such as insti tutes for hotel 
management, catering and food crafts, entrepreneurs hip 
development, nursing and para-medical, civil aviati on related 
training, fashion, design and industrial training. 
A. number of tax concessions under the existing pro visions of Section 10A 
and 10AAof the Income Tax Act are already available to the IT sector. However, 
one of the important impediments to the development of Software Technology Parks 
or IT related SEZs in the North Eastern Region is the non-availabiligy of trained 
human resources in the North Eastern Region Accordi ngly, tax-benefits as is 
availed under Section 80 IC of the Income Tax Act w ould be extended to IT 
related training centres and IT hardware units. 
II. Incentives for Bio-technology industry: 
The biotechnology industry will be eligible for benefits under NEIIPP, 2007 
as applicable to other industries.

[16 May, 2007] .    RAJYA SABHA 
III Incentives for Power Generating Industries: 
Power Generating plansts will continue to get incentives as governed by the 
provisions of Section 81A of the Income Tax Act. In addition, power generating 
plants upto 10 MW based on both conventional and no n-conventional sources 
will also be eligible for capital investment subsid y, interest subsidy and 
comprehensive insurance as applicable under NEIIP, 2007. 
(xii) Establishment of a monitoring mechanism for implementation of 
theNEIIPP,2007: 
In order to establish a monitoring mechanism for implementation of NEIIP, 
2007, a 'High Level Committee'/an Advisory Committee' under the Chairmanship 
of Secretary, Department of Industrial Policy and P romotion and comprising 
Secretaries of the Ministries/Departments of Revenu e, Department of 
Developmet of North Eastern Region (DONER), Banking  and insurance, 
Representative of Planning Commission, CMD, NEDFI a s we" as major 
stakeholders including the industry associations of the North Eastern region would 
be constituted. In addition, an 'Oversight Committee' will be constituted under the 
Chairmanship of the Union Commerce and Industry Min ister with Industry 
Ministers of NE States as its members. 
(xiii) Value Addition 
In order to ensure genuine industrial activities in the North Eastern Region, 
benefits under NEIIPP 2007 will not be admissible to goods in respect of which 
only peripheral activities like preservation during storage, cleaning operations, 
packing, re-packing, labelling or re-labelling, sorting, alteration of retail sale 
price etc. take place.

in the case of Union of India Vs. Mohd Aslam. The matter is at present sub-

Undertrials in various prisons 
†4509. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of HOME  AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many persons accused in various cases are behind 
bars for several years in various prisons of the country; 
(b) if so, the State-wise details of the accused in various jails imprisoned for 
more than six months in various States; and 
(c) whether all the long-imprisoned accused persons are not eligible for bail? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAI RS 
(SHRI MANIKRAO GAVIT): (a) and (b) The total number  of undertrials 
under detention at the end of 2005 as per the data compiled by the National Crime 
Records Bureau (NCRB) were 2,37,076. The State-wise details by period of their 
detention are indicated in the given Statement (See below). 
(c) Offences are categorized as bailable and non-ba ilable. The bail 
provisions for undertrial prisoners are regulated by Section 436,436A, 437 and 439 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. Under section 436 A of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure where an undertrial prisoner other than the one accused of an 
offence for which death has been prescribed as one of the punishments, has been 
under detention for a period extending to one-half of the maximum period of 
imprisonment, provided for the alleged offence, he should be released on his 
personal bond, with or without sureties. It also provides that in no case will an 
undertrial prisoner be detained beyond the maxium period of imprisonment for 
which he can be convicted for the alleged offence. 
Section 436 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has also been 
amended to make a mandatory provision that if the a rrested person is accused 
for a bailabie offence and he is an indigent and ca nnot furnish surety, the 
Court shall release him on his execution of a bond without sureties. 
Further section 437 of the Cr. P.C, provides circumstances in which bail 
can be granted in case of non-bailable offence. Whe n any person accused of, 
or suspected of, the commission of any non-bailable  offence is arrested or 
detained without warrant by an officer-in-charge of a police station or appears or 
is brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, he may 
be released on bail, subject to certain conditional ities as given in section 437 
of the Cr. P.C.

144

the Scheme of Backward Regions Grant Fund (BRGF).

4554. PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to promote production of bio-diesel 
in the country as a substitute for fossil fuel;

proposed by Government to achieve the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SHEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Mi nistry of Rural 
Development has been identified as the nodal Minist ry for processing the 
recommendations of the Planning Commission's Commit tee on the 
Development of Bio-fuel (2003). The Committee recommended launching of a 
National Mission on Bio-Diesel with special focus on the plantation of jatropha, 
the seed of which forms the feedstock for productio n of bio-diesel.

plantation of 5 lakh hectares of bio-fuel plantation over a period of 5 years.

bio-diesel production and marketing on commercial s cale. Under the 
demonstration phase of the national mission on bio- diesel, which is expected 
to be co-terminus with the Eleventh Five Year Plan, about 6 lakh metric tones of 
bio-diesel is likely to be produced annually from the 5 lakh hectares of bio-fuel 
plantation.

Statement II  
Categories of works to be undertaken under NREG  
As per Section 1 of Schedule 1 of National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 
2005, the focus of the Scheme shall be on the following works in their order of 
priority:— 
(i) water conservation and water harvesting; 
(ii) drought proofing (including afforestation and tree plantation); 
(iii) irrigation canals including micro and minor irrigation works; 
(iv) provision of irrigation facility to land owned  by households 
belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes or to land of 
beneficiaries of land reforms or that of the benefi ciaries under the 
Indira Awas Yojana of the Government of India; 
(v) renovation of traditional water bodies including desilting of tanks; 
(vi) land development; 
(vii) flood control and protection works including drainage in water         
logged areas; 
(viii) rural connectivity to provide all-weather access; and 
(ix) any other work which may be notified by the Central Government in 
consultation with the State Government. 
Latest BPL list  
4562. SHRIMAT IHEMAMALINI: 
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: 
SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the latest BPL lists all over the country have been prepared; 
(b) if so,the details thereof, State-wise; 
(c) whether Government have received any complaints reg arding 
anomalies in the said lists; 
(d) if so, the measures taken to sort out such anomalies; 
202 

[16 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) by when the final lists of BPL are likely to be pub lished, particularly in 
Rajasthan; 
(f) whether the number of BPL families in Rajasthan has  incresed or 
decreased during each of the last three years; and 
(g) the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) to (e) After the 
vacation of the stay order by the Hon'ble Supreme C ourt on14.2.2006. the 
finalisation of BPL lists on the basis of BPL Censu s 2002 is being monitored 
regularly. The States of Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand. Madhya 
Pradesh, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and Uttarakhand have already finalized the BPL 
lists. In the remaining States, the work is at vari ous stages and the States have 
been advised to finalise the said lists by the end of June, 2007. The Ministry has 
already issued the guidelines to the States to ensu re the transparency in 
preparation of BPL lists by getting it approved by the Gram Sabha and to 
minimize the subjectivity element. In order to remo ve the anomalies in the 
preparation of the BPL lists and to redress the public grievances, if any, a two-
stage appeal mechanism has already been provided. 
(f) and (g) The BPL Census is generally conducted after a period of 5 years. 
The objective of BPL Census is to identify the BPL households in the rural 
areas for trargeting them under the programmes of t he Ministry and not to 
determine the number of BPL households. The States have been advised to 
identify the number of rural BPL households as dete rmined by the official 
estimates of Planning Commission. The Government of Rajasthan has yet not 
finalized the new BPL lists. 
New BPL list from States  
4563. SHRI K.P.K. KUMARAN: Will the Minister of RUR AL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) how many States have so far submitted New BPL lists , to the Rural 
Development Ministry; 
(b) whether Government propose to extend the two months grace time, 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [16 May, 2007] 
allowed to the Defaulting States, because the frequ ency of Gram Sabha 
Meetings may not synchronies with this time limit; 
(c) whether the real reason for this default is the controversy over the criteria 
for categorization of people as BPL and APL; and 
(d) whether Government would relax the conditions of stoppage of Central Funds 
for Rural Development works, because it may end in retardation 
.  and regression? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYA KANTA PATIL): (a) and ( b) Seven 
States have already finalized the new BPL lists on the basis of BPL Census 2002. 
The progress of finalisation of BPL lists is being monitored/reviewed with the State 
Governments regularly. Last such review was done du ring the meeting of the 
Performance Review Committee held on 12th & 13th Ap ril, 2007. The States 
have been advise to complete the new BPL lists poss ibly by the end of June, 
2007 after getting it approved by the Gram Sabha. T he public grievances are 
also to be redressed through the two-stage appeal mechanism before finalizing 
the BPL lists. 
(c) and (d) The methodology for BPL Census 2002 is score based ranking 
of the rural households for which 13 scorable socio -economic parameters 
have been prescribed. This methodology brings out t he comparative level of 
deprivation of a rural household in an objective manner, therefore, the element of 
subjectivity has been minimized. No State has raised any major objection to the 
above methodology. The Ministry has not yet resorted to any penal action such 
as complete stoppage of Central funds for rural dev elopment works for non-
finalisation of new BPL lists.

DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government had promised t o provide drinking 
water to the remaining 74,000 habitations, that are uncovered by 2008-09 under 
Bharat Nirman;

three quarters of 2006-07, for Accelerated Rural Wa ter Supply Programme 
and how many households have been provided with dri nking water facilities; 
and

Comprehensive Action Plan 99 (CAP 99) based on coverage in previous years,

Wider consultation on Land Acquisition Act, 1894  
4567. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to refer to answer to Starred Question 240, given in 
the Rajya Sabha on 14th March, 2007 and state: 
(a) whether Government have made any efforts to invite concerned people to give 
their views on issues related to Land Acquisition Act of 1894; 
(b) if not, what are the reasons for restricting discus sions only to State 
Governments; 
(c) whether Government would consider inviting views from the Forum on 
Social and Human Rights, to elaborate changes sought and difficulties being faced 
by the poor farmers and backward classes; and 
(d) the steps proposed to carefully weigh proposals for the new Relief Policy, 
and give them weightage, based on their practical utility? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) to (d) Wide-ranging consultations have been 
held by this Ministry in revising the National Poli cy on Resettlement and 
Rehabilitation for Project Affected Families-2003. The draft National 
Rehabilitation Policy-2006 (NRP-2006) was circulate d to the States, UTs and 
concerned departments of the Government of India for comments. Also, the draft 
NRP-2006 was placed in the public domain on the websites of the Department of 
Land Resources as well as the Ministry of Rural Dev elopment. Public notices 
were issued in leading national and regional newspa pers, inviting comments 
from the general public on the draft. Copies of the  draft were also made 
available to the public, free of charge, at the fac ilitation counter of the 
Ministry at Krishi Bhawan, New Delhi. Comments from  a number of non-
governmental organizations as well as from the public at large were received, 
which were examined 
228 

[16 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
and duly taken into consideration in revising of the draft policy. Thus, it is not 
true that the discussions were confined only to the State Governments. 
Also, a meeting with a group of people from outside  the Government who 
have been actively involved in rehabilitation matters was held by this Ministry. 
Thus, ample avenues for offering comments on the subject have been provided to 
the public. 
The draft policy is being finalized with the object ives of minimizing 
displacement and promoting, as far as possible, non -displacing or least 
displacing alternatives, considering social impact assessment (SIA) of projects 
above defined thresholds, ensuring adequate rehabil itation packages and 
expeditious implementation of the rehabilitation pr ocess with the active 
participation of the displaced persons. Necessary a mendments to the Land 
Acquisition Act, 1894 are also being examined. However, the matter is not yet 
finalised.

    (b) if so, the details thereof; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES ( SHRI 
E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) The Government of Maharashtra has requested 
the Government of India to increase the import duty  without specifying the 
level. 
(b) The Government of Maharashtra has stated that d ue to nominal 
levey of import duty at 10%, cotton is being import ed at large scale, affecting 
the prices of cotton and interest of cotton cultiva tors and, further desired 
for incentives as well as increase in import duty. 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [16 May, 2007] 
(c) Ministry of Textiles does not find it reasonable to agree to the demands 
of Government of Maharashtra to enhance the import duty in view of the 
following facts:— 
At present, cotton imports to the extent of 5 to 6 lakh bales are taking place in 
the country mainly in Extra Long Staple (ELS) varie ties of cotton which are 
already in short supply in the country. This is not a large quantity in view of the 
domestic production at around 270 lakh bales. Moreo ver, cotton imports are 
linked to short supply situation and at 10% import duty and for those varieties 
which are not domestically produced. Cotton imports are primarily linked to short 
supply situation especially ELS cotton. In case of the import duty is increased 
to 60%, the domestic industry will ultimately suffer, as it will get ELS cotton at 
enhanced prices. It will further result in enhancement of the cost of production 
of good quality fabrice thereby making Indian textile industry incompetitive in 
domestic as well as international market.

farmers/rural community. Government of India and St ate -Governments should, 
initially extend substantial help towards payment of premiums by farmers as this 
insurance coverage would go a long way towards grad ual elimination of trend of 
resorting to suicides. Let Panchayats/Block officia ls,' NGOs, etc. motivate rural 
folk towards this direction and also evolve modalities through self-help groups so

Need to bridge the gap between rural and urban India  
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA (Rajasthan): Mr Deputy Chairman, Sir, India 
Infrastructure Report 2006, based on a NCEAR's study, shows that the Indian 
metros may be shining, but rural India is still in the dark in four crucial sectors, 
particularly, telecommunications, power water and roads. A dismal 1.67 per cent 
people have telephone connections in villages, while figure for cities is 25.9 per 
cent. A staggering 2,17,000 villages do not have safe drinking water and 55 per 
cent villages are off the surfaced road track. As f or power, much of rural India 
lives in darkness. The old adage about two Indians (Bharat and India) moving 
on parallel track is buttressed by this report, whi ch shows just how 
disconnected the two really are. 
This scenario of discrimination and disparity cannot continue for long. As the 
Indian economy is booming, everyone has the right t o expect a piece of the 
cake. As spurt in economic growth cannot be meaningful if only half of India is 
smiling. 
Your honour a nation cannot be half slave and half free. Hence, I would make a 
submission to the hon. Prime Minister to take necessary steps to bridge the gap 
between the great divide, that is, rural and urban India. Thank you, Sir.
